messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 52

He remembers the morning clearly—the way the light fell across the steel beams, the low rumble of the crane, the scent of wet concrete. He was standing at the edge of the site, reviewing a structural detail on his tablet, when the world shifted. A cable snapped with a sound like a gunshot, and the boom of the crane swung wildly. He watched a worker—a young man he’d spoken to maybe three times—get caught in the arc. There was no scream, just a thud and then silence. He was the first to reach him, but there was nothing to do. The man’s eyes were open, and the architect still sees them every night.

At work now, he avoids the job site. He tells his partners he prefers the office, that he’s too busy with drawings. But the truth is, the smell of diesel and the sound of heavy equipment make his chest tighten. He finds himself checking the load ratings on plans three, four times, even for projects he’s done for years. His junior architect asked him to review a simple column connection last week, and he spent an hour calculating and recalculating the same number, his mind drifting back to that cable snapping. He knows it’s irrational—the accident was a mechanical failure, nothing to do with his design—but he can’t stop the loop.

At home, his wife says he’s not the same. She’s right. He used to come home and talk about a building’s proportions, the way light moved through a lobby. Now he sits in the dark after dinner, scrolling through news articles about construction accidents. He’s edgy. Last week, when their son dropped a glass in the kitchen, he shouted before he could stop himself. The look on the boy’s face—he saw that worker’s eyes again. He apologized, but the distance is growing.

Sleep is a problem. He lies awake replaying the seconds before the snap, wondering if he could have noticed something, shouted a warning. He knows logically he couldn’t have, but the thought claws at him. When he does sleep, he dreams of cranes falling, of buildings turning to dust. He wakes up sweating, heart hammering, and then he can’t fall back. So he gets up and goes to his home office, where he draws by the dim light of a desk lamp. He finds himself sketching the same beam detail over and over, as if he can fix it on paper.

He stopped going to lunch with colleagues. The noise of the cafeteria, the conversations about deadlines and budgets—it all feels meaningless. He started drinking more, just a couple of beers at night, but it’s become three or four. His wife hasn’t said anything, but he sees her watching him.

He feels hollow. Not sad, exactly, but like something essential has been taken out of him. He used to love the precision of his work, the satisfaction of a building rising from plans. Now when he looks at a structure, he only sees what could go wrong. He drives a different route home to avoid the construction site. He avoids heights. He avoids the news. But he can’t avoid the moment—it’s always there, beneath the surface, waiting for a crane’s silhouette or the sound of metal on metal to pull him back.

He’s here because his wife made an appointment. He doesn’t think talking will help, but he’s tired of being this way. He sits in the chair, hands on his knees, and starts to tell the story again, hoping this time it might mean something different.
